newsitem.title: USA: U.S. "perplexed" by EU statements on meat talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. "perplexed" by EU statements on meat talks.

text.p: The United States is perplexed by tough statements made earlier Friday by officials in Brussels regarding bilateral meat talks, and U.S. officials accused EU offficials of "playing to their domestic audience."
"The U.S. is perplexed as to why the EU is making more aggressive statements at this point," said Jim Petterson, an Agriculture Department spokesman. "It's simply not helpful."

An EC spokesman said in Brussels that EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler had recalled negotiators from Washington due to lack of progress in settling the dispute over meat imports. He said Fischler would call USDA Secretary Dan Glickman "to make it clear that the EU's room for manuever has been exhausted."
Petterson said the statements sound like politics on the part of the Europeans. "The bottom line is that it sounds like they're playing to their domestic audience," he said.

Petterson said USDA officials were especially perplexed about the statement that EU negotiators were "recalled," since they were told before the talks began that EU officials would have to leave Thursday afternoon due to personal commitments of Lars Hoelgaard, the EU's lead negotiator.

In a briefing with reporters Thursday before his departure, Hoelgaard said he was disappointed that this week's talks did not settle the issue, but noted that some progress had been made. Head U.S. negotiator Paul Drazek later echoed Hoelgaard's remarks in an interview with Reuters, and said that while differences remained, the talks were constructive.

Petterson said Glickman is willing to talk with Fischler about the dispute or consider an exchange of letters. He said no decision has been made on whether U.S. officials will go to Brussels next week to continue the talks, but that it is under consideration.
"Our goal is to get some sort of agreement, and if it takes going to Brussels to do that, we'd look at that," he said.

U.S. and EU officials have been trying to reach an agreement in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks before April 30, by which Washington has warned it will remove over 100 European meat and poultry plants from its list of approved exporters if the issue has not been resolved by then.

The delisting of the plants would halt some $300 million worth of Euoprean meat shipments to the United States, mostly pork products from Denmark. U.S. poultry shipments to Europe have been halted since April 1 due to new regulations imposed by the EU. The United States normally exports around $50 million worth of poultry to EU annually.
